gamut

GAM-ut · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Gamut is the complete range or scope of something.

The new restaurant's menu runs the gamut from simple grilled cheese to elaborate seven-course tasting plates.

Example

During the trial, the witness's testimony ran the gamut from confident and detailed to confused and contradictory within a single afternoon.

Gamut almost always appears in the phrase 'run the gamut,' describing something that covers every possibility from one extreme to another.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

range: A range is the stretch between two limits -- a price range, a range of sizes -- and it can be narrow or partial. The gamut is always the whole stretch: every possibility from one extreme all the way to the other, with nothing left outside it.

scope: Scope is how far something extends -- the scope of an investigation, a project's scope. It draws the outer boundary of what is covered, and that boundary can be wide or tight. The gamut is not a boundary but the full spread inside one, from extreme to extreme.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

narrowness: a very limited range or extent

limitation: a restriction on the extent of something

Where it sits · how fully it spans the possibilities

variety → gamut → entirety

variety vs. gamut: Variety is a weaker claim than the gamut: it means several different kinds are present, without promising that everything between the two extremes is covered.

entirety vs. gamut: Entirety goes further than the gamut -- it means absolutely all of one single thing, nothing left out at all, while a gamut is specifically the spread running between two opposite extremes.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — gamma ut: the lowest note of the medieval musical scale (Medieval Latin, from Greek letter gamma + the note 'ut')

Put it together: Gamut began as a medieval music term -- gamma ut, the very lowest note on the old musical scale -- and came to mean the entire scale of notes, then any complete range of anything at all.

Where it comes from: Gamut fuses two medieval music syllables: gamma (the Greek letter, used as a note name) and ut (the lowest note of the old scale). The name of that single bottom note stretched to cover the whole run of notes, and then any complete range you can imagine.
